items.title: UK Chancellor John Healey struck a notably upbeat tone in his first major speech today, aiming to turn Great Britain into “Growth Britain." While maintaining Rachel Reeves’ commitment to strict fiscal discipline, he broadened the economic lens to unlock regional investment—particularly across the North—and lower business costs. (He noted that if debt interest were a Whitehall department, it would outspend Defense, the Home Office, and Justice combined.) The real test remains translating this into durable policy adoption before rising borrowing costs further squeeze both growth and the public finances. #economy #markets #growth #UK

items.title: These charts are from the New York Fed paper titled "Are Central Banks Moving Out of Dollar Assets?" It finds that the fall in the share of the dollar in official foreign reserves around the world, from 64% in 2015 to 56% in 2025, "reflects the actions of a handful of large reserve holders" rather than "a systemic global shift away from dollar assets." It will be interesting to see what happens to both the magnitude and the composition by the end of this year. #economy #markets #dollar #centralbanks @NewYorkFed

items.title: The latest US jobs report came in significantly stronger than expected across both sides of the labor market: demand and supply. Specifically: Job Creation: Nonfarm payrolls surged from an upwardly revised 21,000 to 162,000, roughly three times the consensus forecast. Labor Supply: The labor force participation rate rose from 61.4% to 61.6%, beating expectations and marking its strongest level in nearly a year. Other Key Indicators: The unemployment rate held steady at 4.1%, while average hourly earnings rose 0.3% month-over-month, matching expectations. Together, these indicators point to a US labor market that remains robust with firm demand and is stabilization on the supply side. #econom
items.content:
The latest US jobs report came in significantly stronger than expected across both sides of the labor market: demand and supply.
Specifically:
Job Creation: Nonfarm payrolls surged from an upwardly revised 21,000 to 162,000, roughly three times the consensus forecast.
Labor Supply: The labor force participation rate rose from 61.4% to 61.6%, beating expectations and marking its strongest level in nearly a year.
Other Key Indicators: The unemployment rate held steady at 4.1%, while average hourly earnings rose 0.3% month-over-month, matching expectations.
Together, these indicators point to a US labor market that remains robust with firm demand and is stabilization on the supply side.
 #economy   #jobs   #earnings   #employment   #unemployment 
— Mohamed A. El-Erian (@elerianm) Sep 4, 2026
